planting.note: Separate bulbs into cloves and plant pointed-end-up 2 inches deep about a month before the ground freezes so roots form before winter dormancy.

directions: Russian Red is a cold-hardy hardneck long grown in the Pacific Northwest from stock originally brought over from Russia, producing a tall central scape and a moderate number of large, easy-to-peel cloves wrapped in reddish-brown-streaked skins. It wants a genuine winter chill to divide properly into cloves, so it performs best where soil freezes at some point each year. Cut or snap off the curling scape once it makes a loop or two to redirect energy into bulb size, and harvest when the lower several leaves have browned while a few green ones remain. Cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks before trimming and storing.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange growing guide

planting.note: Plant large cloves 2-3 inches deep and well spaced in fall, since this porcelain type forms big bulbs with relatively few but substantial cloves.

directions: Pskem traces to the Pskem River valley in the Tian Shan mountains of Uzbekistan and is classed as a porcelain hardneck, forming a tall woody scape and a bulb wrapped in smooth white skin over just four to six oversized cloves. The outsized cloves make it a favorite for cooks who dislike peeling many small pieces, though the plant itself demands more spacing and richer soil than smaller-clove types to reach full size. Remove the scape once curled to push growth into the bulb, and wait to harvest until the lower leaves have browned while several upper leaves stay green. Cure in a shaded, ventilated space for three to four weeks before trimming roots and tops for storage.
sources: Peaceful Valley Farm Supply growing guide

planting.note: Plant cloves in fall in free-draining soil; Brown Saxon matures earlier than many hardnecks and tolerates milder, wetter winters than the coldest-climate types.

directions: Brown Saxon is an English heirloom hardneck with tan to light-brown bulb wrappers and a reliably mild, rounded flavor compared to sharper continental types, making it popular for growers in cooler, damper maritime climates where many hardnecks struggle. It bulks up a bit faster than late-season porcelain types, so watch for scapes to form and remove them promptly to concentrate growth in the bulb. Harvest once the lower leaves begin to brown, lift carefully to avoid bruising the relatively thin skins, and cure in a dry, shaded, airy location for a few weeks before storing. Because it is less cold-tolerant than extreme-climate hardnecks, gardeners in very harsh winter regions should mulch the planting bed well.
sources: The Garlic Farm (Isle of Wight, UK) variety guide

planting.note: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in fall, well before the ground freezes, in loose fertile soil to let this productive porcelain type size up fully.

directions: Shantung Purple traces to Shandong province in China and is grown as a porcelain-type hardneck, forming smooth white-skinned bulbs sometimes blushed with purple streaking around five to seven plump cloves. Growers favor it for consistent bulb size and good yields compared to some finickier heirloom porcelains. Snap off the scape once it curls to direct energy into the bulb, and harvest when the lowest few leaves have browned while upper leaves remain green. Cure for several weeks in a shaded, well-ventilated spot before trimming and storing in a cool, dry place.
sources: Washington State University Extension garlic production guide
